newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CSR, Mackay sugar j/v approved by ACCC. [CORRECTED 03:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: CSR, Mackay sugar j/v approved by ACCC. [CORRECTED 03:00 GMT]

text.p: The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) said on Wednesday it had approved a plan for a sugar refining joint venture between CSR Ltd and Mackay Refined Sugar Pty Ltd.
The announcement came in an ACCC statement released through the Australian Stock Exchange.

The ACCC said the planned removal of sugar tariffs was a significant factor in the decision, which was an effective reversal of a 1993 decision by the ACCC's predecessor, the Trade Practices Commission (TPC) to block and earlier joint venture plan.
(Corrects to make clear that the announcement made by the Australian Stock Exchange came from the ACCC not CSR Ltd.)
"The joint venture will cover purchasing, refining, storage, distribution and sale of refined sugar domestically and internationally," the ACCC said.
Milling assets were not part of the joint venture, it said.
The ACCC said the 1993 decision was taken because it was not satisfied the joint venture would result in a public benefit substantial enough to outweigh the anti-competitive effect.
"At that time, refined sugar imports were not considered by the TPC to be an effective competitive constraint on domestic refiners," ACCC Chairman Professor Allan Fels said in the statement.
"A tariff of $55 per tonne on raw and refined sugar imports, together with high freight costs, placed imports at a substantial competitive disadvantage," he said.
"Since 1993, there have been significant developments in the industry which have increased the effectiveness of imports as a competitive constraint on domestic refiners."

"The removal of the tariff, as recommended by the Commonwealth, Queensland and industry Sugar Industry Review Working Party, was a significant factor in today's decision. In addition, evidence supplied to the ACCC supported the claim that freight rates have fallen considerably over the past 18 months while there continues to be an expansion in world and regional refined sugar capacity," the ACCC said.
"The ACCC considers that these factors place imports in a position to compete more favourably with domestic refined sugar."
The regulator also said it believed there would be sufficient excess capacity in the industry to prevent any attempt by the joint venture to increase prices significantly.

CSR and MRS had provided the ACCC with an enforceable undertaking that the joint venture would make existing import facilities in Western Australia available, at cost, to other Australian refiners and importers.
